item.title: Engram MCP: Zero-Dependency Persistent Memory for AI Coding Agents
item.description: Engram MCP is a zero-dependency Go binary that gives AI coding agents persistent memory via SQLite + FTS5, supporting 12+ agents with 20 MCP tools.
item.content:encoded:
What is Engram MCP?

Engram MCP is an open-source, zero-dependency persistent memory system for AI coding agents built as a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server. Written in Go and distributed as a single binary, Engram gives AI agents the ability to remember information across sessions, conversations, and even different machines — without requiring Node.js, Python, Docker, or a vector database. Created by Gentleman-Programming in February 2026, it has rapidly become the most popular AI agent memory solution on GitHub with over 5,700 stars and 605 forks in just five months.

Why AI Agents Need Persistent Memory

Every developer who has worked with AI coding agents has experienced the frustration: you tell the agent your project structure, coding conventions, and architecture decisions in one session, only to have it forget everything when you start a new one. This is the session amnesia problem — the fundamental limitation of stateless AI interactions.

Without persistent memory, AI agents operate in a vacuum. Each session starts from scratch, forcing developers to repeatedly explain project context, preferred patterns, and past decisions. This wastes time, introduces inconsistency, and limits the agent’s ability to act as a true long-term coding partner.

Persistent memory solves this by giving agents a durable storage layer they can read from and write to across sessions. When an agent can remember that you prefer async/await over raw promises, that your API follows a specific error-handling pattern, or that a particular module was refactored last week, it transitions from a stateless autocomplete tool to a genuine collaborative partner.

Architecture Deep Dive

Engram’s architecture is deliberately minimal. The entire system is a single Go binary that communicates with AI agents through MCP’s stdio transport protocol. Here is how it works under the hood:

Go Binary with Pure Go SQLite. Engram is written in Go and uses modernc.org/sqlite — a pure Go SQLite implementation that requires no CGO, no GCC, and no system-level SQLite libraries. This is what makes the zero-dependency promise real: you download one file, make it executable, and it runs on any Linux, macOS, or Windows system.

SQLite + FTS5 Backend. Instead of spinning up a vector database like ChromaDB, Pinecone, or Qdrant, Engram uses SQLite with its built-in FTS5 full-text search extension. FTS5 provides fast, ranked full-text search over stored memories without any external dependencies. The design decision is deliberate: for the vast majority of agent memory use cases — recalling past decisions, project conventions, code patterns, and configuration preferences — keyword search with FTS5 covers 95% of needs without the complexity, cost, and latency of embedding-based vector search.

MCP stdio Transport. Engram runs as a subprocess of the AI agent, communicating over standard input/output using the Model Context Protocol. This means no network ports to configure, no servers to manage, and no authentication tokens to set up. The agent launches Engram, and the two processes exchange structured messages through a pipe.

20 MCP Tools. Engram exposes 20 distinct MCP tools organized into several categories:

Category Tools Purpose
Save mem_save, mem_save_batch Store new memories with optional tags and priority
Search mem_search, mem_search_similar Retrieve memories by keyword or semantic similarity
Context mem_context, mem_context_clear Manage working context for the current session
Session mem_session_start, mem_session_end, mem_session_list Lifecycle management for memory sessions
Conflict mem_judge, mem_resolve, mem_diff Surface and resolve conflicting memories
Utility mem_stats, mem_export, mem_import, mem_clean, mem_backup, mem_restore, mem_config, mem_status Maintenance, migration, and introspection

This comprehensive tool set means agents can not only store and retrieve memories but also manage session boundaries, detect conflicts between old and new information, and perform maintenance operations — all through the same MCP interface.

20 MCP Tools: Full Breakdown

The 20 MCP tools in Engram cover the full lifecycle of agent memory management:

Save Tools. mem_save stores a single memory with optional tags, priority level, and source attribution. mem_save_batch allows bulk storage of multiple memories in one call, useful when an agent processes a large codebase and wants to record many observations at once.

Search Tools. mem_search performs FTS5 full-text search across all stored memories, returning ranked results with relevance scores. mem_search_similar uses the FTS5 ranking to find semantically related memories based on content overlap — a lightweight alternative to vector embeddings.

Context Tools. mem_context retrieves the most relevant memories for the current working context, automatically filtering by recency and relevance. mem_context_clear resets the working context when switching tasks or projects.

Session Tools. mem_session_start begins a new memory session, creating a logical boundary for related memories. mem_session_end closes the current session. mem_session_list enumerates all sessions, allowing agents to navigate between different work contexts.

Conflict Tools. mem_judge surfaces memories that contradict each other — for example, if an agent was told to use tabs in one session and spaces in another. mem_resolve lets the agent or user pick the correct version. mem_diff shows the difference between conflicting memories.

Utility Tools. mem_stats provides memory usage statistics. mem_export and mem_import enable memory migration between Engram instances. mem_clean removes stale or low-priority memories. mem_backup and mem_restore provide snapshot-based backup and recovery. mem_config reads or modifies Engram’s runtime configuration. mem_status returns the health and state of the memory store.

Agent Compatibility

Engram is designed to be agent-agnostic — it works with any MCP-compatible AI coding agent. The supported agents include:

Agent Setup Method Notes
Claude Code MCP config file Add Engram as an MCP server in claude_desktop_config.json
Codex MCP config file Works with Codex CLI via stdio transport
Gemini CLI MCP config file Google’s agent supports MCP stdio servers
Cursor MCP config file Add in Cursor’s MCP server settings
Windsurf MCP config file Configure in Windsurf’s MCP settings panel
VS Code Copilot MCP config file Via VS Code MCP extension support
OpenCode MCP config file Open-source agent with MCP support
Antigravity MCP config file Experimental agent with MCP compatibility
Qwen Code MCP config file Alibaba’s coding agent
Kiro MCP config file Lightweight coding agent
Kilo Code MCP config file VS Code extension with MCP support
Pi MCP config file General-purpose AI agent

The setup is identical across all agents: download the Engram binary, point the agent’s MCP configuration to the binary path, and the agent gains persistent memory capabilities immediately.

Competitor Comparison

The MCP memory ecosystem has grown rapidly, with over 10 competing projects on GitHub. Here is how Engram stacks up against the main alternatives:

Feature Engram Nocturne Memory Stash MegaMemory Phantom
Stars 5,712 1,278 759 305 1,454
Language Go Python Go TypeScript Python
Dependencies None Python runtime Postgres Node.js Python runtime
Backend SQLite + FTS5 Graph-like Postgres In-process embeddings Custom
Search FTS5 keyword Graph traversal SQL Semantic Custom
License MIT MIT Apache-2.0 MIT Custom
Binary Size ~10 MB N/A ~10 MB N/A N/A
Cloud Sync Optional No No No Yes
Git Sync Yes No No No No
Agent Count 12+ Any MCP Any MCP Any MCP Single agent

Engram leads in adoption (5,712 stars), zero-dependency architecture, and unique features like Git sync and two-layer privacy stripping. Nocturne Memory offers a graph-based alternative for structured memory relationships. Stash provides a Postgres-backed solution for teams already running Postgres. MegaMemory brings semantic search with in-process embeddings. Phantom is more of a full AI assistant than a pure memory layer.

Zero-Dependency Advantage

The single-binary approach is Engram’s most distinctive technical advantage. Here is why it matters:

No Runtime Requirements. Competing solutions require Node.js (MegaMemory, AgentRecall-X), Python (Nocturne, Phantom), Docker (EngramMemory/engram-memory), or Postgres (Stash). Engram requires nothing — not even a Go runtime, since it is compiled to a static binary.

Instant Setup. Download the binary, chmod +x, configure the MCP path, and you are done. There is no npm install, pip install, docker pull, or apt-get step. This makes Engram ideal for CI/CD pipelines, ephemeral development environments, and air-gapped systems.

Cross-Platform Consistency. Because Engram bundles its own SQLite (via modernc.org/sqlite), the behavior is identical on every platform. There is no risk of version mismatches between system SQLite libraries or missing FTS5 support.

Small Footprint. The Engram binary is approximately 10 MB — tiny compared to a Node.js runtime (~50 MB), Python interpreter (~30 MB), or Docker image (~200 MB+). This matters for resource-constrained environments like edge devices, containers, and cloud functions.

No Port Conflicts. Since Engram uses MCP stdio transport, there are no network ports to manage. Multiple Engram instances can run simultaneously without port conflicts, each attached to a different agent session.

SQLite + FTS5 vs Vector Databases

One of Engram’s most debated design decisions is using SQLite FTS5 instead of vector embeddings. Here is the trade-off:

When FTS5 Wins. For the majority of agent memory use cases, keyword search is sufficient. When an agent needs to recall “the error handling pattern we agreed on” or “the database schema for the user model,” FTS5 full-text search finds the relevant memory quickly and accurately. FTS5 supports ranked results, prefix queries, and phrase matching — all without generating a single embedding vector.

When Vector Search Wins. For fuzzy semantic matching — “find memories similar to this concept” without knowing the exact keywords — vector embeddings provide better recall. If an agent needs to find “all memories related to authentication” but the stored memories use terms like “login,” “OAuth,” “JWT,” and “SSO,” vector search would surface them all while FTS5 might miss some.

The Pragmatic Verdict. Engram’s approach covers 95% of real-world agent memory use cases with zero embedding costs, zero API calls, and zero infrastructure. For the remaining 5% where semantic search is genuinely needed, Engram’s mem_search_similar tool uses FTS5’s built-in ranking to approximate semantic matching. Projects that require true vector search can look at MegaMemory (in-process embeddings) or EngramMemory/engram-memory (Qdrant + FastEmbed).

Privacy and Data Control

Engram takes a privacy-first approach to agent memory with a two-layer stripping architecture:

Plugin-Level Stripping. Before a memory reaches the storage layer, the MCP plugin strips sensitive information — API keys, tokens, file paths, and personally identifiable information — from the memory content. This happens at the agent integration level, before data is transmitted to Engram.

Store-Level Stripping. The storage layer applies a second round of sanitization, catching anything the plugin layer might have missed. This defense-in-depth approach ensures that sensitive data never persists in the memory store.

Local-First by Default. All memories are stored in a local SQLite database on the user’s machine. No data leaves the local system unless the user explicitly opts into cloud sync. This contrasts with cloud-dependent memory services like Mem0 and Zep, which require sending memory data to external servers.

Full Data Portability. Because memories are stored in a standard SQLite database, users have complete access to their data. The mem_export and mem_import tools allow migration between Engram instances, and the raw SQLite file can be queried with any SQLite client.

Git Sync and Cross-Machine Memory

One of Engram’s most innovative features is Git-based memory synchronization. Here is how it works:

Compressed Chunk Storage. Memories are stored as compressed chunks rather than individual files. This keeps the storage efficient and avoids the problem of thousands of tiny files that plagues file-based memory systems.

No Merge Conflicts. Because Engram uses a chunk-based approach with append-only semantics, there are no merge conflicts when syncing between machines. Each machine’s memories are additive — new chunks are added, and conflicts are resolved at the application level rather than the file level.

Cross-Machine Workflow. A developer can work on their desktop in the morning, commit memory changes to a Git repository, and pull those memories on their laptop in the afternoon. The agent on the laptop has full context of the morning’s work without any manual transfer.

Team Collaboration. Multiple developers working on the same project can share memory through a shared Git repository. When one developer’s agent learns a project convention or discovers a bug pattern, that knowledge propagates to the entire team’s agents through Git sync.

Cloud Integration

For users who want cloud-based memory synchronization without managing Git repositories, Engram offers opt-in cloud replication:

Project-Scoped Sync. Cloud sync is organized by project, not by user. This means memories are scoped to the project context, preventing cross-project contamination.

Local SQLite Remains Authoritative. Even with cloud sync enabled, the local SQLite database remains the primary data store. The cloud is a replication target, not a source of truth. This ensures that the system works offline and that the user always has full control over their data.

Encrypted Transport. Cloud sync uses encrypted channels to protect memory data in transit. The two-layer stripping ensures that even if the transport were compromised, sensitive data would not be exposed.

Getting Started

Getting started with Engram takes less than five minutes:

Step 1: Download the Binary. Download the latest Engram release from the GitHub releases page. Choose the binary for your operating system and architecture.

Step 2: Make It Executable. Run chmod +x engram on Linux or macOS. On Windows, the binary runs directly.

Step 3: Configure Your Agent. Add Engram as an MCP server in your agent’s configuration. For Claude Code, this means adding an entry to claude_desktop_config.json:

{
  "mcpServers": {
    "engram": {
      "command": "/path/to/engram",
      "args": ["mcp"]
    }
  }
}

Step 4: Save Your First Memory. Ask your agent to remember something: “Save that I prefer async/await over .then() chains.” The agent calls mem_save through MCP, and the memory is stored in the local SQLite database.

Step 5: Verify Persistence. Start a new session and ask: “What do I prefer for async code?” The agent calls mem_search, finds the stored memory, and applies it — no re-explanation needed.

Verdict

Engram MCP is the best choice for developers and teams who want persistent AI agent memory without infrastructure overhead. Its zero-dependency design, SQLite + FTS5 backend, and agent-agnostic compatibility make it the most accessible memory solution in the MCP ecosystem.

Choose Engram if: You want instant setup, no runtime dependencies, local-first privacy, and compatibility with any MCP-compatible agent. It is ideal for individual developers, small teams, and anyone who values simplicity and data control.

Consider alternatives if: You need true semantic vector search (MegaMemory or EngramMemory/engram-memory), you are already running Postgres and want a SQL-backed solution (Stash), or you prefer graph-based structured memory (Nocturne Memory).

With 5,712 GitHub stars, 20 MCP tools, support for 12+ agents, and a thriving open-source community, Engram has established itself as the de facto standard for AI agent persistent memory in 2026.

FAQ

Q: Does Engram require an internet connection? A: No. Engram is fully local-first. All memories are stored in a local SQLite database on your machine. Cloud sync is optional and opt-in only.

Q: Can Engram work with multiple agents simultaneously? A: Yes. Engram is agent-agnostic and can be configured with any MCP-compatible agent. Each agent instance gets its own Engram process via stdio transport.

Q: How does Engram handle conflicting memories? A: Engram provides dedicated conflict tools — mem_judge surfaces contradictions, mem_diff shows the differences, and mem_resolve lets the agent or user pick the correct version.

Q: Is Engram free to use? A: Yes. Engram is MIT-licensed open-source software. There are no paid tiers, no API costs, and no usage limits. Cloud sync is also free and optional.

Q: What happens to my memories if I uninstall Engram? A: Your memories are stored in a standard SQLite database file. You can back it up with mem_backup, export it with mem_export, or simply copy the SQLite file before uninstalling. The data is fully portable.

item.title: Agent Memory Layer Comparison 2026: Déjà Vu vs Mem0 vs Zep vs Agent Memory MCP
item.description: Compare Déjà Vu, Mem0, Zep, and Agent Memory MCP — the top agent memory layer solutions in 2026 across performance, privacy, pricing, and architecture.
item.content:encoded:
Introduction — Why Agent Memory Matters in 2026

Agent memory is the single most important infrastructure decision for production AI agents in 2026. Without a persistent memory layer, every agent conversation starts from scratch — no user preferences, no session history, no learned behaviors. The four leading solutions — Déjà Vu, Mem0, Zep, and Agent Memory MCP — take fundamentally different approaches to solving this problem, and choosing the wrong one can cost you in latency, privacy, vendor lock-in, or benchmark credibility. This comparison breaks down each solution’s architecture, performance, pricing, and ideal use case so you can make an informed decision for your agent stack.

The Four Contenders at a Glance

The agent memory layer market in 2026 has fragmented into four distinct categories, each with a different philosophy about how agents should remember.

Déjà Vu — Retroactive Session Log Indexing

Déjà Vu is a zero-dependency Go binary that takes a radically different approach from every other memory solution: it does not capture anything. Instead, it indexes agent session logs that already exist on disk. Built by vshulcz, it supports over eight agent harnesses including Claude Code, Codex, opencode, aider, Gemini CLI, Cursor, Antigravity, and Grok Build. Its warm search latency is an astonishing 7-9ms typical, with a worst-case of ~40ms over gigabytes of logs. The index compresses to roughly 2.4% of the original corpus size — a 1GB log directory becomes a 24MB index. Déjà Vu is privacy-first by design: there is no network path in its indexing or search code, and credentials are redacted at index time. It also ships an MCP recall tool for agent self-querying and auto-recall via SessionStart hooks.

Mem0 — Cloud-Native Semantic Memory Platform

Mem0 is a Y Combinator-backed cloud memory layer that uses a semantic graph to link user profiles with preference nodes. It performs autonomous semantic extraction from conversational streams, building a structured knowledge graph of user preferences, facts, and relationships over time. Mem0 integrates with LangChain, CrewAI, and other popular agent frameworks. However, it is cloud-only — requiring an API key and costing $40-50+ per month. Mem0 published benchmark results claiming state-of-the-art performance on the LoCoMo benchmark, though those claims have been contested by Zep with evidence of implementation errors in Zep’s evaluation.

Zep — Temporal Knowledge Graph Memory

Zep offers both an open-source Community Edition and a commercial Cloud tier. Its core innovation is Graphiti, a temporal knowledge graph that tracks fact validity over time using valid_at and invalid_at metadata on graph edges. This temporal awareness is critical for agents that need to know not just what a user said, but whether that information is still current. Zep asynchronously precomputes graph and related facts for low-latency deterministic retrieval, supports a full CRUD API for fine-grained data control, and recently added Attribute-Based Access Control (ABAC) for enterprise security compliance. The Community Edition was open-sourced in September 2024 and has seen rapid adoption.

Agent Memory MCP — The Protocol Standard

Agent Memory MCP is not a memory platform itself but a protocol — the Model Context Protocol — that has become the universal connector for agent memory tools. MCP defines a standard interface for agents to read from and write to memory servers, enabling a plug-and-play ecosystem where any MCP-compatible memory backend can be swapped in without changing agent code. Déjà Vu ships an MCP recall tool, Zep offers MCP integration, and the protocol is rapidly becoming the lingua franca of agent memory. For teams building multi-agent systems, MCP compatibility is increasingly a non-negotiable requirement.

Head-to-Head Comparison

Architecture & Storage Model

Feature Déjà Vu Mem0 Zep Agent Memory MCP
Core approach Retroactive log indexing Semantic graph extraction Temporal knowledge graph Protocol standard
Storage On-disk index (~2.4% of corpus) Cloud-hosted graph DB Local or cloud graph DB Depends on backend
Data model Flat search index User-preference graph Temporal graph with edge timestamps Abstracted by protocol
Capture mechanism None (reads existing logs) Autonomous extraction from streams Async graph precomputation Via MCP server
LLM in CRUD path No Yes No (precomputed) Depends on server
Temporal awareness No (static index) Limited Full (valid_at/invalid_at) Depends on server

Déjà Vu’s architecture is the simplest: it indexes what agents already wrote to disk. There is no capture step, no running service, and no cloud dependency. This makes it ideal for developers who want zero infrastructure overhead. The trade-off is that it has no temporal awareness — it cannot distinguish between a preference stated yesterday and one stated six months ago.

Mem0 builds a semantic graph by extracting entities and relationships from conversation text using an LLM. This means every memory write incurs an LLM call, adding latency and cost. The graph structure enables rich relationship queries — “what does this user prefer in Italian restaurants?” — but the cloud dependency means your agent’s memory stops working if the API is unreachable.

Zep’s temporal knowledge graph is the most sophisticated storage model. Every fact is stored with valid_at and invalid_at timestamps, enabling the agent to answer time-sensitive questions like “what was the user’s shipping address last month?” The graph is precomputed asynchronously, so reads are deterministic and low-latency without requiring an LLM in the critical path.

Agent Memory MCP abstracts the storage model entirely. Your agent talks to an MCP server, and the server handles whatever backend it uses. This is the most flexible option but adds a protocol layer that may introduce latency.

Latency & Performance Benchmarks

Metric Déjà Vu Mem0 Zep Notes
Read latency (typical) 7-9ms ~200-500ms (LLM-dependent) ~50-100ms Déjà Vu is 10-50x faster
Read latency (p95) ~40ms Not published 0.632s (concurrent) Zep’s published figure
Index/build time Fast (Go binary) N/A (real-time) Async precomputation Déjà Vu indexes offline
Memory overhead ~2.4% of corpus Cloud-hosted Cloud or local Déjà Vu is most efficient
Concurrent search Single-threaded Cloud-scaled 0.632s p95 Zep published concurrent data

Déjà Vu’s performance numbers are remarkable: 7-9ms typical warm search and ~40ms worst-case over a 3.3GB corpus of 1,250+ sessions. This is possible because it is a pure Go binary with no network calls and no LLM involvement. The index is a flat, optimized structure designed for fast keyword and semantic search.

Zep’s published p95 search latency is 0.632s for concurrent searches, compared to Mem0 Graph’s 0.657s — a statistical tie. However, Zep argues that its temporal knowledge graph provides richer, more accurate results that justify the comparable latency.

Mem0’s latency is harder to benchmark because every memory operation may involve an LLM call for entity extraction. In practice, users report 200-500ms per operation, with significant variance depending on the LLM provider and network conditions.

Privacy & Data Sovereignty

Aspect Déjà Vu Mem0 Zep Agent Memory MCP
Data location Local disk Cloud servers Local (CE) or Cloud Depends on server
Network required No Yes Optional Optional
Credential handling Redacted at index time Server-side Configurable Depends on server
Open source Yes No Yes (CE) Yes (protocol)
Self-hostable Yes No Yes (CE) Yes

Privacy is where the solutions diverge most dramatically. Déjà Vu is the clear winner for privacy-conscious teams: it has no network path in its indexing or search code, credentials are redacted at index time, and the entire system runs on local disk. Your agent’s memory never leaves your machine.

Mem0 is at the opposite end of the spectrum. As a cloud-only service, all conversation data is processed and stored on Mem0’s servers. For teams subject to GDPR, HIPAA, or other data residency requirements, this may be a dealbreaker.

Zep offers a middle path. The Community Edition is fully self-hostable and open-source, giving you data sovereignty. The Cloud tier adds enterprise features like ABAC and managed infrastructure. This makes Zep suitable for organizations that want control but may not want to operate their own graph database.

Agent Memory MCP is protocol-level and inherits the privacy posture of whatever server you choose. You can run a local MCP memory server for full privacy or connect to a cloud MCP server for managed infrastructure.

Pricing & Deployment Models

Solution Pricing Deployment Best for
Déjà Vu Free (open-source) Local binary Solo devs, privacy-first teams
Mem0 $40-50+/month Cloud-only Teams already in cloud ecosystem
Zep CE Free (open-source) Self-hosted Teams wanting control + features
Zep Cloud Usage-based Managed Enterprise teams
MCP Memory Free (protocol) Any Teams wanting flexibility

Déjà Vu and Zep Community Edition are both free and open-source, but they serve different needs. Déjà Vu is a lightweight binary you run alongside your agent — no database, no dependencies. Zep CE requires running a graph database but offers richer memory features.

Mem0’s $40-50+/month pricing may seem modest, but it adds up across multiple agents and environments. For a team running five agents in production, that is $200-250/month for memory alone.

Framework & Harness Support

Déjà Vu leads in harness support with compatibility for Claude Code, Codex, opencode, aider, Gemini CLI, Cursor, Antigravity, and Grok Build. Mem0 integrates with LangChain and CrewAI. Zep offers SDKs for Python and TypeScript with integrations for LangChain, LlamaIndex, and direct API access. Agent Memory MCP is framework-agnostic — any agent that speaks MCP can use any MCP-compatible memory server.

The Benchmark Controversy: LoCoMo vs LongMemEval

The agent memory field is currently embroiled in a benchmark war that reveals deeper problems with how we evaluate memory systems. Zep published a detailed critique of the LoCoMo benchmark, which Mem0 had used to claim state-of-the-art performance.

Zep’s analysis identified three fundamental flaws in LoCoMo. First, the benchmark conversations average only 16,000-26,000 tokens — well within the context window of modern LLMs. This means a model with a large context window could theoretically answer memory questions without any external memory system at all, making the benchmark a test of context length rather than memory quality. Second, LoCoMo does not test knowledge updates — it cannot distinguish between a system that remembers a fact correctly and one that fails to update when that fact changes. Third, Zep identified data quality issues in the benchmark dataset.

When Zep ran its own evaluation correcting for these issues, it achieved a 75.14% J score on LoCoMo compared to Mem0 Graph’s approximately 68% — a roughly 10% advantage. Zep also claims that Mem0’s evaluation of Zep had implementation errors including an incorrect user model, improper timestamp handling, and sequential instead of parallel searches.

Zep advocates for LongMemEval as a superior alternative. LongMemEval features significantly longer conversations averaging 115,000 tokens, which better stress-test real memory systems. It also includes temporal reasoning tasks that require the system to track how facts change over time — something LoCoMo does not test.

The takeaway for practitioners: do not make purchasing decisions based on LoCoMo scores alone. The benchmark is widely considered insufficient for evaluating production memory systems. If you are evaluating memory layers, design your own evaluation that reflects your actual use case — conversation lengths, update patterns, and query types that match your deployment.

The Emerging Three-Tier Architecture

A consensus is forming among production agent teams that a single memory layer is insufficient. The emerging best practice is a three-tier architecture:

Tier 1: Session Log Memory (Zep or custom). This is the raw message database with auto-summarization and message-indexing pipelines. It captures the full conversation history and provides search over past interactions. Zep is the leading solution for this tier, but a custom implementation using a vector database is also common.

Tier 2: Personalization Memory (Mem0 or equivalent). This is a semantic graph linking user profiles with preference nodes. It extracts and stores user preferences, habits, and personal facts. Mem0 dominates this tier, but Zep’s temporal graph can also serve this role.

Tier 3: Governance Memory (ContextNest or custom). This is a deterministic, version-controlled memory layer that uses SHA-256 hash chains and steward approval for compliance-critical applications. Unlike the probabilistic approaches of Zep and Mem0, governance memory provides auditable, tamper-proof records of what the agent knew and when.

The PromptOwl framework explicitly recommends deploying all three layers together. In this architecture, Zep manages session logs, Mem0 handles personalization, and ContextNest provides governance. Each layer handles the type of memory it is best suited for, and together they form a complete memory stack.

The Local-First Movement in Agent Memory

A significant trend in 2026 is the shift toward local-first agent memory, driven by three factors: privacy concerns, cost optimization, and latency requirements.

Déjà Vu is the purest expression of this movement. By indexing existing session logs with no capture step, it eliminates the need for any cloud service or running daemon. Its privacy-first design — no network path, credential redaction at index time — makes it the go-to choice for developers who cannot or will not send agent conversation data to third parties.

Zep Community Edition supports this trend by offering a self-hosted alternative to cloud-only solutions. Teams can run Zep on their own infrastructure, keeping all data in-house while benefiting from the temporal knowledge graph.

Mem0’s cloud-only model is increasingly at odds with this trend. While its semantic graph capabilities are compelling, the requirement to send all conversation data to Mem0’s servers is a hard block for many enterprise deployments. The market is voting with its feet: open-source, self-hostable solutions are gaining adoption faster than cloud-only alternatives.

MCP as the Universal Memory Connector

The Model Context Protocol (MCP) is rapidly becoming the universal connector for agent memory tools. Originally developed by Anthropic, MCP defines a standard interface for agents to interact with external tools and data sources, including memory.

Déjà Vu ships an MCP recall tool that enables agents to query their session history through the MCP protocol. Zep offers MCP integration for its temporal knowledge graph. The protocol enables a plug-and-play ecosystem where any MCP-compatible memory backend can be swapped in without changing agent code.

For teams building multi-agent systems, MCP compatibility is increasingly a non-negotiable requirement. It allows different agents — potentially using different frameworks — to share a common memory interface. An agent built with LangChain and an agent built with Claude Code can both access the same MCP memory server, sharing context and learned preferences.

The MCP ecosystem is also enabling new memory paradigms. Serverless memory solutions like Mnemora, which achieves sub-10ms state reads with four memory types (state, semantic, episodic, procedural) and requires no LLM for CRUD operations, are emerging as MCP-compatible backends. This gives teams the flexibility to start with a simple MCP memory server and upgrade to a more sophisticated backend as their needs grow.

How to Choose the Right Memory Layer

The right memory layer depends on your specific requirements. Here is a decision framework:

Choose Déjà Vu if: You need zero infrastructure overhead, your agents already write session logs to disk, privacy is a hard requirement, and you do not need temporal awareness or real-time memory capture. Déjà Vu is ideal for solo developers, research projects, and teams that want to add memory to existing agent workflows without changing their architecture.

Choose Mem0 if: You are building a user-facing application that needs rich personalization, you are already in a cloud ecosystem, and you are willing to pay $40-50+/month for managed memory infrastructure. Mem0’s semantic graph excels at extracting and serving user preferences, but the cloud dependency and LLM-in-the-loop cost are significant trade-offs.

Choose Zep if: You need temporal awareness — the ability to track when facts were true and when they changed — or you want the flexibility of an open-source Community Edition with an enterprise Cloud upgrade path. Zep is the most balanced option, offering sophisticated memory features with deployment flexibility.

Choose Agent Memory MCP if: You are building a multi-agent system, you want to avoid vendor lock-in, or you need the flexibility to swap memory backends without changing agent code. MCP is not a memory solution itself but the protocol that connects agents to memory — pair it with any backend that meets your requirements.

For most production deployments in 2026, the recommended approach is a hybrid: use MCP as the protocol layer, Zep CE or Déjà Vu for local-first memory, and supplement with a cloud service for specific personalization needs. The three-tier architecture — session log, personalization, and governance — provides the most complete memory solution for serious agent deployments.

Conclusion — The Future of Agent Memory

The agent memory layer market in 2026 is vibrant and fragmented, with no single solution dominating. Déjà Vu’s retroactive indexing, Mem0’s cloud semantic graph, Zep’s temporal knowledge graph, and the MCP protocol each serve different needs in the agent memory stack.

Three trends will shape the future. First, the local-first movement will continue to gain momentum as privacy regulations tighten and teams seek to reduce cloud dependencies. Second, MCP will become the universal memory connector, enabling plug-and-play memory backends. Third, the three-tier architecture — session log, personalization, and governance — will become the standard for production deployments.

The benchmark controversy around LoCoMo versus LongMemEval highlights a deeper issue: the field needs better, more realistic evaluation standards. Until then, practitioners should design their own evaluations based on their specific use cases rather than relying on published benchmark scores.

The bottom line: agent memory is no longer optional for production AI systems. Choose your memory layer carefully, test it against your actual workloads, and design for the flexibility to evolve as the field matures.

FAQ

Q1: What is the fastest agent memory layer in 2026? Déjà Vu is the fastest by a wide margin, with 7-9ms typical warm search latency and ~40ms worst-case over gigabytes of session logs. This is because it is a pure Go binary with no network calls and no LLM involvement in the search path. Zep and Mem0 are both significantly slower due to their graph database and LLM dependencies.

Q2: Is Mem0 really state-of-the-art for agent memory? The claim is contested. Mem0 published SOTA results on the LoCoMo benchmark, but Zep published a detailed critique showing that Mem0’s evaluation of Zep had implementation errors. When Zep ran corrected evaluations, it achieved a 75.14% J score versus Mem0 Graph’s ~68%. The LoCoMo benchmark itself has been criticized for insufficient conversation length and lack of temporal reasoning tests.

Q3: Can I use agent memory without sending data to the cloud? Yes. Déjà Vu is fully local with no network path in its indexing or search code. Zep Community Edition is open-source and self-hostable. Agent Memory MCP can be paired with a local MCP memory server. Only Mem0 requires cloud connectivity.

Q4: What is the three-tier memory architecture for AI agents? The three-tier architecture consists of session log memory (raw conversation history with search, typically Zep), personalization memory (semantic graph of user preferences, typically Mem0), and governance memory (deterministic, version-controlled records with audit trails, typically ContextNest). Production agents should deploy all three layers together for complete memory coverage.

Q5: How does MCP change agent memory? MCP (Model Context Protocol) provides a standard interface for agents to read from and write to memory servers. This enables a plug-and-play ecosystem where any MCP-compatible memory backend can be swapped in without changing agent code. It is becoming the universal connector for agent memory, allowing multi-agent systems to share a common memory interface regardless of the framework each agent uses.
